main.t: The flat, triangular shoulder blade at the back of the shoulder (scapula).

simpler.t: The scapula is your shoulder blade.

deeper.t: With the clavicle it forms the shoulder (pectoral) girdle, which anchors the arm to the trunk.

facts.t: It lies at the back of the shoulder.
Muscles lie in front of it and behind it, so it does not touch the ribs.
Outwards, it meets the humerus at the shoulder joint and the clavicle at the tip of the shoulder.

simpler.t: It sits on your upper back, behind your shoulder.

deeper.t: It has no joint with the ribs. Muscles cover it on both sides.

items.name: Glenoid cavity
items.t: The shallow socket for the head of the humerus.

items.name: Spine
items.t: The ridge across the back. With the acromion and clavicle it makes a V-shaped line for muscles.

items.name: Acromion
items.t: The flat outer end of the spine. It is the bony tip of the shoulder and meets the clavicle.

items.name: Coracoid process
items.t: A hook at the front shaped like a crow’s beak. It anchors chest and arm muscles and a strong ligament.

items.name: Supraspinous, infraspinous and subscapular fossae
items.t: Broad hollows. They give large areas for muscles that move the arm.

items.name: Inferior angle
items.t: The lowest corner. Several powerful muscles of the shoulder and arm attach here.

items.name: Supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles
items.t: Small bumps above and below the socket, for arm muscles.

items.name: Suprascapular notch
items.t: A notch in the top border. The suprascapular nerve passes through it.
items.check: OpenStax gives the notch’s position; the nerve passing through it is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

simpler.t: It has a shallow socket for the arm bone, a ridge across the back and two hooks at the top.

deeper.t: The spine, acromion and clavicle form a V-shaped line where neck and back muscles attach.

facts.t: Its socket is shallow, so the arm can move very widely. The cost is a less stable joint.
A small rim of fibrocartilage (glenoid labrum) deepens the socket slightly.
Its broad hollows and ridges give big areas for the muscles that move and steady the arm.
It is not joined to the ribs by bone. It moves with the clavicle as one unit.

simpler.t: Its shallow socket lets your arm move freely, and its wide surfaces hold strong muscles.

items.name: Rotator cuff
items.t: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis start on the scapula and attach to the humerus.

items.name: Shoulder (glenohumeral) joint
items.t: Ball-and-socket joint between the glenoid cavity and the head of the humerus.

items.name: Acromioclavicular joint
items.t: Where the acromion meets the clavicle. Its own ligaments are fairly weak.

items.name: Coracoclavicular ligament
items.t: A very strong band from the coracoid to the clavicle. It gives the acromioclavicular joint its main support.

items.name: Subacromial bursa
items.t: A fluid sac that stops the rotator cuff tendons rubbing on the scapula.

items.name: Long thoracic nerve
items.t: Supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall.

simpler.t: The muscles that hold the shoulder joint together start on the scapula.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification), like all girdle bones except the clavicle.
In some adults part of the acromion never fuses to the rest (os acromiale). It can be mistaken for a fracture.

items.injury: A strong blow to the outer shoulder, such as a player driven into the boards.
items.damaged: The acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments tear (a “shoulder separation”).
items.cannotDo: Hold the shoulder up: it droops.
items.why: The scapula separates from the clavicle and the weight of the arm pulls it down.

items.injury: Repeated use with the arm raised out to the side, as in throwing, swimming or racquet sports.
items.damaged: The rotator cuff tendons, bursae or glenoid labrum.
items.cannotDo: Raise and use the arm without pain.
items.why: These tendons and the bursae become inflamed or torn with repeated use in raising the arm.

items.injury: Injury to the long thoracic nerve.
items.cannotDo: Push against a wall without the scapula sticking out (“winging”).
items.why: Serratus anterior holds the scapula flat against the chest wall.

items.q: Explain how the shape of the scapula trades stability for mobility at the shoulder.
model: The glenoid cavity is small and shallow: about a third of the size of the humeral head.
The joint capsule is thin and loose.
The glenoid labrum deepens the socket only slightly.
The rotator cuff muscles give the main support, acting as “dynamic ligaments”.

items.q: A rugby player lands on the point of the shoulder. Predict the injury and what you would see.
model: Dislocation of the acromioclavicular joint (shoulder separation).
Both the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments rupture.
The acromion is forced under the end of the clavicle.
The shoulder droops as the weight of the arm pulls the scapula down.

items.q: Compare the coracoid process and the acromion.
model: Coracoid: a hook at the front that curves forwards and outwards.
It anchors chest and arm muscles and the coracoclavicular ligament.
Acromion: the flat outer end of the spine of the scapula.
It forms the tip of the shoulder and meets the clavicle.

check.stem: Which part of the scapula forms the bony tip of the shoulder?
check.why: The acromion is the flat outer end of the spine of the scapula and forms the tip of the shoulder.

check.stem: Which ligament gives the acromioclavicular joint its main support?
check.why: The very strong coracoclavicular ligament anchors the coracoid process to the underside of the clavicle.

check.stem: Why does the scapula not touch the ribs?
options: It is held away by the clavicle alone
A layer of cartilage separates them
It sits above the level of the ribs
Muscles lie both in front of it and behind it
check.why: Muscles cover it on both sides, so it does not articulate with the ribs of the thoracic cage.
